prompt.context: The CEO of Chemicals Inc., a leading chemicals company with a long history of innovative products and application technologies has contacted you for assistance. In the past couple of years, the company's bottom-line profitability has slowly eroded to the point where EBITDA is hovering barely above 0, even though the company's overall sales growth is outpacing industry averages. Magnifying these financial problems are the reports he is receiving from his business unit leaders which are that revenues and volumes are up and profitability has never been higher.
prompt.question: The CEO looks at you across the table and asks: 'What do I do?'

clarifying_info.q: Tell me about the firm's product portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: Many different kinds of chemicals products, sold to many different kinds of customers (large, small), in many different kinds of industries (automotive, medical, consumer products), all around the globe.

The company is organized geographically and by the underlying technologies that drive products, not necessarily by product line. Definition of product line is technology-application (think industry)-geography, e.g. Chemical A – Automotive – USA.

clarifying_info.q: What industries are customers of the firm's products?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive, Medical, Consumer Products (packaging), Manufacturing, Electronics, Drilling.

clarifying_info.q: How does the firm view the world in terms of regions?
clarifying_info.a: North America, South America, Europe, Pacific.

clarifying_info.q: Who are their competitors? What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: Major competitors include large multi-national corporations as well as small, local, specialized firms with a single product. Some of these firms actually purchase our client's products and rework them and sell to the end customer.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs the company is incurring?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues last year were $2Bn. The COGS is variable, about 25%, but all companies in this industry are dealing with fluctuating feedstock prices. SG&A expense is 30% of revenue and beyond the industry benchmark. Other costs are inline with industry norms.

exhibits.title: Product Line Contribution Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart displaying contribution margins across 15 product lines. Each bar represents a distinct product line; bar colors correspond to the business unit (Technology A, B, or C) that owns that product line.
exhibits.data: 15 product lines spanning three chemical technologies (A, B, C) and five industry verticals; contribution margins vary widely across product lines with no clear clustering by business unit color.

framework: Customers: who are they, where are they, what do they buy and how price-sensitive are they by industry?
Product & Service Mix: which product lines are profitable vs. commoditized; are services uniformly applied regardless of product margin?
Cost Structure: assess COGS (variable ~25%, feedstock exposure) and SG&A (~30% of revenue, above industry benchmark); investigate cost allocation across business units
Organization: evaluate whether current BU structure (by technology) aligns incentives with profitability; explore whether a cost allocation problem is masking corporate-level losses
Pricing: assess whether the firm is undercharging for specialized products and services relative to customer willingness to pay

questions.prompt: What is driving the disconnect between business-unit-level profitability and corporate-level EBITDA near zero?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will hypothesize a cost allocation problem: BUs report strong margins because shared costs (SG&A, services) are not properly allocated down to BUs. They should also consider that some product lines may be subsidizing others.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What insight do you draw about the product portfolio?
questions.guidance: Candidates should observe the wide range of contribution margins across the 15 product lines, indicating significant commoditization of parts of the portfolio. They should note that business unit colors are spread across the full contribution margin range — meaning each BU owns both high-margin and low-margin lines — and suggest realigning product lines by margin tier rather than by technology.

questions.prompt: Given the SG&A is 30% of revenue and above the industry benchmark, what might be causing elevated SG&A?
questions.guidance: The firm provides the full suite of services (small batch sizes, custom logistics, technical/customer support, application development support) to every product line regardless of its contribution margin. High-cost services are being applied equally to low-margin commodity products and high-margin specialty products, inflating SG&A without commensurate return on commodity lines.

math.setup: Revenue = $2Bn; COGS = 25% of revenue = $0.5Bn; SG&A = 30% of revenue = $0.6Bn; total COGS + SG&A = $1.1Bn; EBITDA ≈ 0 implies remaining costs ≈ $0.9Bn leaving almost no profit. SG&A alone at $0.6Bn is a major cost driver.
steps: Remaining for other costs and EBITDA ≈ $900M, with EBITDA near 0 meaning other costs ≈ $900M or SG&A is the primary lever
math.answer: SG&A at $600M on $2Bn revenue is the key controllable cost that is above industry benchmark and represents the primary profitability lever.

questions.prompt: How are different customer industries characterized in terms of price sensitivity and service needs?
questions.guidance: Automotive: price conscious except safety/interior applications. Consumer Goods/Packaging: very cost conscious, cannot pass costs on. Electronics: need inexpensive products but willing to pay more for small lot sizes and specialized custom technical support. Medical: specialized applications (e.g., lenses), can pass costs to customers. Drilling: huge cost of broken parts, want the best products regardless of price. Strong candidates will link these needs to a tiered service model.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional changes might you consider to an organization facing increased commoditization of their product lines, and how might the organization reduce volatility in raw materials costs?

categories.name: Combating commoditization
ideas: Invest in R&D to develop next-generation specialty products with higher barriers to entry
Move up the value chain by offering application development and co-engineering services
Pursue long-term contracts or preferred supplier status with high-value customers (Medical, Drilling)
Develop industry-specific sales teams that span business units to deepen customer relationships
Consider divesting or outsourcing the most commoditized product lines
Build a brand/certification around quality for safety-critical applications

categories.name: Reducing raw materials cost volatility
ideas: Hedge feedstock prices using commodity derivatives
Negotiate long-term supply contracts with feedstock suppliers to lock in prices
Develop alternative feedstock sources or substitutes
Vertical integration into key raw material supply
Pass through feedstock price changes contractually to customers via price escalation clauses
Build strategic inventory buffers to smooth cost peaks

recommendation: Reorganize the company into two business units: Specialty (high-margin product lines) and Commodity (low-margin product lines)

The Specialty BU should continue to provide a high level of customized service; the Commodity BU should adopt a low-cost service model (IT-enabled tools, a la carte service agreements, less favorable terms and conditions)

Develop a shared service model: embed BU-specialized functions into each business unit and retain general functions (legal, HR, facilities) in a corporate core; assign a single accountable leader to each shared service responsible for cost incurrence and allocation; shared function leaders should negotiate service-level agreements with BU leaders
risks: Appropriate classification of product lines to Specialty vs. Commodity BU now and over time as margins shift
Business units do not own manufacturing and supply chain, so these remain holders of unnecessary cost with little incentive to optimize
Reduced personal service to commodity customers may make the company less competitive and reduce top-line revenue and volume
next_steps: Study manufacturing and supply chain to allocate these costs to business units where practical
Increase partnerships with specialty chemicals customers to grow volume in high-margin business
Consider outsourcing or divesting one business unit to focus the firm; or develop a portfolio strategy with major customers such as industry-specific sales teams that span business units
